title: Service Boundaries
subtitle: Decomposing systems along Domain-Driven Design Bounded Contexts to maximize cohesion and minimize coupling.
keyTakeaways: Service boundaries should be drawn along Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Bounded Contexts, not technical layers or single database tables.
The Distributed Monolith antipattern occurs when services share databases or require lock-step deployments, adding network latency without any autonomy benefits.
Conway's Law dictates that system architecture mirrors organizational communication structure; cross-functional teams must own services end-to-end.

sections.heading: DDD Bounded Contexts and Conway's Law
sections.body: Decomposing a system into microservices based on arbitrary technical layers (such as a 'Database Service', 'Business Logic Service', and 'UI Service') is an architectural antipattern that guarantees tight coupling. Effective service boundaries align with Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Bounded Contexts. A Bounded Context encapsulates a specific business sub-domain with its own ubiquitous language and domain model. For example, a 'User' in the Authentication context means email and password hash; in the Fulfillment context, 'User' means shipping address and delivery preferences.
bullets: High Cohesion, Loose Coupling: Operations that change together frequently should reside in the same service. Interactions crossing service boundaries should represent stable, asynchronous domain events.

Conway's Law: Organizations design systems that mirror their communication structure. Assigning a single service to a cross-functional team (Frontend, Backend, SRE) prevents inter-team deployment blockades.

sections.heading: Avoiding the Distributed Monolith and Nano-Services
sections.body: Splitting an application into 50 microservices before business domain boundaries are well understood creates a Distributed Monolith. A distributed monolith shares all the disadvantages of a monolith (tight coupling, fragile releases) combined with all the disadvantages of distributed systems (network partitions, serialization latency, distributed transactions).
bullets: The Lock-Step Deploy Test: If deploying Service A requires deploying Service B at the same time, they are not independent microservices; they are a distributed monolith.
Nano-Service Antipattern: A service that contains barely 100 lines of code to wrap a single database table incurs excessive network hop overhead and operational maintenance.

Monolith-First Strategy: Mature engineering organizations build a modular monolith first. Once domain boundaries stabilize and team size expands, extract high-load or high-change modules into independent microservices.

tradeOffs.pros: Autonomous deployments; independent horizontal scaling; fault isolation across business domains.
tradeOffs.cons: Network latency between services; eventual consistency; distributed tracing and monitoring complexity.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large engineering organizations (50+ engineers) with multiple independent product squads.

tradeOffs.pros: Sub-millisecond in-memory function calls; single database with full ACID transactions; simple deployments and debugging.
tradeOffs.cons: Entire application deploys together; bad code can crash the shared process; unified database can become a bottleneck.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Early-stage startups, small teams (<20 engineers), and applications with evolving domain models.

interviewTip: When asked how to split a monolith in an interview, do not immediately draw 20 microservices: 'We will identify Bounded Contexts using Domain-Driven Design. We will start by extracting high-throughput, independently evolving domains—like Payment or Notifications—while keeping tightly coupled core workflows in a modular monolith until team size demands further decomposition.'
